chapter: Prose: All Summer in a Day
trick: The whole story hangs on one ratio: seven years of rain against one hour of sun. Fix that in your head and everything else follows, including why the children could not believe Margot and why shutting her in the cupboard was so cruel.

data.prompt: Put the events of All Summer in a Day back into the order Bradbury tells them.

items.label: The class waits, knowing the sun is due after seven years of rain
items.note: Venus, where it has rained without stopping

items.label: Margot tells them the sun is like a penny, like a fire in the stove
items.note: She alone remembers it, from Earth

items.label: The children refuse to believe her and push her into a cupboard
items.note: They lock the door and run off

items.label: The rain stops and the sun blazes for one hour
items.note: The jungle steams and the children play

items.label: The rain begins again and the children go back indoors
They remember Margot, and stand a long time before opening the door
items.note: Bradbury ends here and does not tell us what she said

chapter: Poem: Mild the Mist upon the Hill
trick: Read the weather as the poet's mood. The mist is mild, the storms are over, the day has already wept its fill. Brontë is describing a calm that comes after grief, not before it, and that is why the poem feels peaceful rather than gloomy.

trick: Tom's plan fails and succeeds at the same time. He does not get out of school, but he walks in with a gap he can spit through, and that gap makes him the most admired boy in the yard. Twain's joke is that Tom always lands on his feet.

data.prompt: True or false? Mark each statement about Tom Loses a Tooth.

items.statement: Tom first pretends that his toe is mortified, hoping to be kept home from school.
items.why: He groans about the toe until Aunt Polly loses patience, and only then does the loose tooth come out in conversation.

items.statement: Aunt Polly pulls the tooth out with a pair of pliers.
items.why: She ties one end of a silk thread to the tooth and the other to the bedpost, then thrusts a piece of fire almost in his face so that he jerks back.

items.statement: Tom is delighted once the tooth is out, because the gap lets him spit in a new way.
items.why: The new accomplishment draws a following of admiring boys, so his loss turns into fame.

items.statement: Tom is glad that his plan to miss school has worked perfectly.
items.why: The plan fails: Aunt Polly sends him to school anyway, and the tooth is gone into the bargain.

items.statement: On his way to school Tom meets Huckleberry Finn.
items.why: Huck, the boy every mother in the town disliked and every boy envied, is on his way with a dead cat.

trick: The seagull does not choose to fly. He is starved into it, and he only notices he is flying after his wings have already caught the air. That is the point of the story: fear ends the moment you act, not before.

trick: Three moves, always the same three. The object comes to the front, the verb becomes a form of BE plus the past participle, and the old subject goes to the back after 'by'. If you cannot find an object in the active sentence, it usually cannot be made passive at all.

video.query: active and passive voice rules with examples class 9 English grammar

data.prompt: Change each sentence from the active voice into the passive.
data.rule: Change the sentence from the active voice to the passive voice, keeping the tense the same.

items.from: The gardener waters the plants every morning.
items.to: The plants are watered by the gardener every morning.
items.hint: Simple present, plural object, so the verb becomes 'are watered'.

items.to: Gitanjali was written by Rabindranath Tagore.
items.hint: Simple past, singular object, so 'was' plus the past participle.

items.from: The children are singing a song.
items.to: A song is being sung by the children.
items.hint: A continuous tense needs 'being' in the passive as well.
When the doer is unknown or unimportant, drop the 'by' phrase altogether.
An imperative turns into 'Let ... be ...' in the passive.
